transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist here. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. So, um, I guess I'm here because... well, things have just been getting really, really difficult for me lately, especially with my program. I'm in school right now—I'm training to be a radiologic tech—and the thing is, I just feel like I'm literally crawling out of my skin whenever I'm supposed to sit still. 

Like, whether I'm in the radiology suite waiting at the console or I'm stuck in a classroom for a long lecture, it’s just this intense, overwhelming physical feeling. I’ve been trying to just tough it out, you know? For months I’ve been telling myself to just sit down and be normal like everyone else, but no matter how hard I try, I just can't do it. I always end up shifting around in my seat a million times, or I'll just stand up and start pacing in the back of the room. In the clinic, I'm constantly finding some random excuse to get up and move around, like pretending I need to check the supply closet or adjust something that doesn't even need adjusting. I just absolutely have to move, and it's exhausting, honestly, just trying to fight it all day, every day. I just can't seem to stay put.

Going back as far as you can remember—say, when you were in elementary school or middle school—did you have this same difficulty sitting still and this need to move around, or is this something that's really only started happening more recently?

Oh, no, definitely not recent. Not at all. If you ask my mom and dad, they'll probably just groan, honestly, because they still talk about these parent-teacher conferences from way back in elementary school. Like, way before middle school even started. 

I guess it was kind of a whole ordeal for them every single year. They'd go in, and the teachers would sit them down in those tiny little chairs and say the exact same thing, like, "He's a sweet kid, but he just absolutely cannot stay in his seat." And it's true, I was always up and wandering around the classroom, looking at the posters, or going to the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or just... I don't know, bothering the kid next to me. 

And it wasn't just the getting up, either. The teachers would always complain that I was constantly calling out in class. Like, the teacher would barely start asking a question and I’d just shout the answer out without raising my hand because I just couldn't hold it in, you know? It felt like the words were just bursting out of my mouth before my brain even caught up. Or, like, they'd hand out a worksheet or an art project or something, and I would just start rushing ahead before they even finished giving the directions. I'd just guess what we were supposed to do because listening to the whole step-by-step explanation took way too long and I just wanted to get my hands on it and do it. Of course, I'd end up doing it completely wrong half the time because I didn't listen to the end, but I just couldn't wait. 

So, yeah, this was happening way, way back then in elementary school. It’s definitely not just something that started since I got into this radiology training. I think it's just that now, the stakes are so much higher, you know? Like, I'm supposed to be this professional adult in a medical clinic, so the fact that I can't sit still feels a lot more serious and embarrassing, but the actual physical feeling? The moving and the rushing? That's been there basically my whole life.

When you were in school back then, and even now—aside from the trouble sitting still and blurting things out—did teachers or people around you ever comment on you having trouble paying attention, or losing focus, or forgetting things you were supposed to do?

No, not really. I mean, it’s always been the moving around that was the big issue, you know? Like, I don’t really remember anyone saying I was spacing out or staring at the wall or anything like that. It was more like... I was too engaged, if that makes sense? Like I was doing too much, too fast, rather than just drifting off. 

I mean, sure, I guess everyone forgets things sometimes, like maybe I’d forget to bring a permission slip home or something, but it wasn’t like a constant thing where teachers were pulling my parents aside to say I was losing my homework or forgetting my assignments. It was always, always about the fact that I was up out of my chair, or talking over people, or just generally causing a ruckus because I couldn’t just be still. 

Even now, like in the clinic, I know exactly what I’m supposed to be doing. I’m not forgetting the protocols for the X-ray machine or losing track of what the doctor asked for. My brain is totally there, and I’m focused on the task. It’s just that my body won’t cooperate with the sitting part of it. If I’m moving, I’m fine. I can pay attention to the screen while I’m standing up and shifting my weight from foot to foot, no problem. It’s just the physical restraint that gets me, not the mental focus part. So, yeah, I wouldn’t say attention or memory has ever really been the main complaint from anyone. It’s always been the physical energy and the blurting things out.

When you were doing schoolwork or tasks that required concentration, like reading a book or doing homework, did you ever find it hard to keep your mind on what you were doing, or did your mind wander to other things even when you were trying to focus?

No, honestly, I don't think so. I mean, if I'm reading something or doing homework, my mind doesn't really wander off to, like, daydreaming or thinking about what I'm going to have for dinner or whatever. It's not like my brain is floating away from the task. It's more like... my brain is right there, totally focused on the book or the assignment, but my body is screaming at me to do something else while I'm doing it. 

Like, if I had to read a chapter for school, I could read it and understand it and tell you exactly what happened, but I would probably be reading it while hanging upside down off the edge of the couch, or pacing back and forth across the living room carpet, or tapping my foot so hard the whole floor shakes. I remember my dad used to get so annoyed because I'd be doing my math homework at the kitchen table, and I'd be getting the answers right, but I'd be constantly getting up to open the fridge, look inside, close it, sit back down, do one problem, get up, walk around the island, sit back down, do another problem. 

So the concentration part? Keeping my mind on the actual work? That was fine. I could do the work. I just couldn't do it while sitting still in a chair like a normal person. It was never a matter of my mind wandering, it was just... my physical energy wandering, I guess? Like I had to burn off this intense, buzzing feeling in my arms and legs just so my brain could do its job. Even now, if I have to study for an exam for my program, I can't just sit at a desk in the library. I have to be on a treadmill or walking around my apartment reading the notes out loud. If I try to just sit and read, I get so physically uncomfortable that I can't stand it, but it's not because I'm losing focus on the material. The focus is there, it's just trapped in a body that won't stop moving.

You mentioned that your mind stays focused on the task even when your body is moving around. But I'm curious—when you're in situations where you have to sit still, like in a classroom or at the clinic console, do you ever find it difficult to concentrate on what's being said or what you're supposed to be doing, or is it purely just the physical discomfort and the urge to move that's the problem?

Yeah, no, it is absolutely, one hundred percent just the physical discomfort. Like, I completely hear what you're asking, but it's not a concentration thing at all. It's purely that physical urge. I mean, if I'm at the clinic console—and this happens all the time, especially when we're doing a longer scan where I literally just have to sit there and watch the monitor—I am totally locked in on the screen. I know exactly what phase the scan is in, I'm watching the contrast, I'm listening to the radiologist if they're in the room, I'm paying attention to the patient's breathing instructions over the intercom. My mind is completely on the job. But my body? It's like... it's like there's this electric current running through my veins, or like a pressure cooker building up steam, and I just desperately need to release it. 

If I force myself to just sit perfectly still like a statue, it honestly physically aches. It's this crawling sensation under my skin, mostly in my legs, but sometimes in my arms too. So I’ll be sitting there, absorbing every single word the doctor or the senior tech is saying, but I’m white-knuckling the edge of the desk, or I’m bouncing my heel so fast the chair is vibrating, or I’m chewing on the inside of my cheek just to channel that energy somewhere. 

And it’s the exact same thing in a classroom. We have these long anatomy and physiology lectures, which, you know, is a long time to sit for anybody, but for me it's basically torture. I’m listening to the professor, I’m taking the notes, I’m getting the material, but the whole time I’m just shifting my weight, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning back, leaning forward, stretching my neck. It’s like wearing a wool sweater that’s three sizes too small and incredibly itchy, and you just want to rip it off and throw it across the room, but you can't because you're in the middle of a crowded lecture hall. You're still paying attention to the lecture, you're not daydreaming, but you're just painfully aware of the sweater, you know? 

So, yeah, it's never that I forget what I'm doing or stop listening or zone out. The concentration is totally fine. It's just that forcing myself not to move takes so much... I don't know, physical willpower? It’s just this intense, overwhelming need to get up and do something, anything, with my body, even though my brain is perfectly happy doing the task at hand. It's just the sitting. The sitting is the absolute worst part.

You've mentioned that when you're interested in something or when it's engaging, you can focus just fine even while moving around. But what about tasks that are boring or repetitive—like filing paperwork, or reading something dry that you're not really interested in? Do you find your mind actually drifting away from those kinds of tasks, even when you're trying hard to pay attention?

No, honestly, even then, it’s not the drifting mind thing. I mean, I know what you’re getting at, like when you hear about people reading a textbook and suddenly they realize they read three pages and don’t remember a single word? People in my cohort talk about that all the time, but I just don’t get that. My brain doesn't do the floating away thing. 

Like, take the daily QA logs at the clinic. It is the most mind-numbing stuff on the planet. You literally just have to run the phantom scans first thing in the morning, input the density numbers into this ancient Excel spreadsheet, make sure the contrast resolution is within baseline... it’s incredibly dry, repetitive work. And I’m doing it, right? I’m looking at the numbers, I’m typing them in, my brain is completely registering that the Hounsfield units are correct, I’m not spacing out or thinking about what I’m gonna do this weekend or staring blankly at the wall. 

But because it’s so boring, the physical part—that need to move—it just dials up to an eleven. It’s like, because my brain isn’t being actively challenged by a real patient or a complex scan, my body decides it needs to throw a party to make up for it. So I’m sitting at the computer in the back office, and I’m clicking the cells, but I’m also rolling the chair back and forth across the floor mat. I’m clicking my pen a thousand times a minute until the receptionist glares at me. I’m getting up to throw away a single tiny piece of scrap paper, then sitting back down, then getting up to check if the printer has paper even though I’m not even printing anything. I’ll stretch my arms all the way to the ceiling, crack my knuckles, bounce my knee so hard the monitor literally shakes on the desk. It’s just this absolute physical chaos. 

But if you asked me right in the middle of all that bouncing and pacing what the last number I typed was, I could tell you instantly. The focus on the spreadsheet is unbroken. I don't lose my place. It’s just that the physical restraint feels a hundred times worse when the task is boring. When it's interesting, the moving is just background noise, but when it's filing or typing logs, the urge to jump out of my skin is all I can feel. So, yeah, no drifting away, no daydreaming, just... just a lot more moving around to compensate for how tedious it is, if that makes sense? Because I really don't have that thing where my brain just shuts off or wanders away. It's always on the task, it's just my body that refuses to deal with the boredom.
